title: The Return to Protectionism
research_question: What were the short-run effects of the 2018 U.S. import tariffs and the retaliatory tariffs imposed by trading partners on U.S. import and export quantities, prices, aggregate real income, and the distribution of welfare across regions and sectors? How were the patterns of protection and retaliation related to political and electoral characteristics of U.S. counties?
data_description: The authors construct a monthly panel data set covering 2017:1–2019:4. Statutory U.S. import tariffs at the HS-8/HS-10 level come from U.S. International Trade Commission schedules; retaliatory tariffs are compiled from official documents of the Ministry of Finance of China, Department of Finance of Canada, Office of the President of Mexico, and WTO filings (covering the EU, Russia, Turkey), at the HS-6 level, combined with WTO MFN tariff data. Monthly U.S. import and export values and quantities by HS-10 product and country (varieties) come from the U.S. Census Bureau, including duties collected. Sector-level data (NAICS-4) include Federal Reserve G17 Industrial Production and BLS PPI/MPI/XPI indices. BEA 2016 input-output tables provide sectoral linkages. County-by-sector employment and wages come from Census County Business Patterns and BEA Local Area Personal Income; demographics from the American Community Survey; and county-level 2016 presidential voting from the FEC.
institutional_context: After decades of U.S. leadership in lowering trade barriers, in 2018 the United States enacted multiple waves of tariff increases authorized under provisions of the Trade Act of 1974 and the Trade Expansion Act of 1962, citing injury to domestic industries, national security, and unfair trade practices. Average statutory tariffs rose from 2.6% to 16.6% on 12,043 products covering $303 billion (12.7%) of annual imports, beginning with solar panels and washing machines in February 2018, followed by steel and aluminum, and successive waves targeting Chinese goods. In response, China, Canada, Mexico, the EU, Russia, and Turkey imposed retaliatory tariffs covering $127 billion (8.2%) of U.S. exports across 8,073 products, raising average rates from 7.3% to 20.4%. Tariffs were largely concentrated at 10% or 25% rate changes, were discriminatory across origin countries, and disproportionately covered intermediate inputs, with retaliations heavily targeting U.S. agriculture.
